front_blocks.md: Define **ATP**.

back_blocks.md: **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide made of **adenine**, **ribose** and **three phosphate groups**; it is the universal energy currency of cells.

front_blocks.md: What features make **ATP** suitable as the universal energy currency?

back_blocks.md: Releases energy in **small, usable amounts**
Releases energy **instantly** in a single reaction (hydrolysis)
Easily **re-formed** from ADP + P<sub>i</sub>
**Soluble** and moves easily within cells

back_blocks.md: By **hydrolysis** of ATP to **ADP** + inorganic phosphate (P<sub>i</sub>), which releases energy.

front_blocks.md: Define **chemiosmosis**.

back_blocks.md: **Chemiosmosis** is the synthesis of ATP driven by the flow of **protons (H^+^)** down their gradient across a membrane in mitochondria and chloroplasts.

front_blocks.md: Define **respiratory substrate**.

back_blocks.md: A **respiratory substrate** is an organic molecule that is **oxidised** during respiration to release energy (e.g. carbohydrate, lipid, protein).

front_blocks.md: Which respiratory substrate has the **highest energy value per gram**?

back_blocks.md: **Lipids** — about **twice** the energy value of carbohydrates or proteins per gram.

front_blocks.md: Explain why **lipids** have a higher energy value than carbohydrates.

back_blocks.md: Lipids contain **more hydrogen atoms** (more C–H bonds) per molecule.
So more hydrogen is available to reduce NAD/FAD, releasing more energy in oxidative phosphorylation.

cards.front_md: Explain why **lipids** have a higher energy value than carbohydrates.

Lipids contain **more hydrogen atoms** (more C–H bonds) per molecule.

So more hydrogen is available to reduce NAD/FAD, releasing more energy in oxidative phosphorylation.

back_blocks.md: More hydrogen atoms produce **more reduced NAD/FAD**, which supply more electrons to the electron transport chain, generating more ATP.

front_blocks.md: Define **respiratory quotient (RQ)**.

back_blocks.md: The **RQ** is the ratio of the number of molecules of **carbon dioxide produced** to the number of molecules of **oxygen taken in** during respiration.

front_blocks.md: Define **respirometer**.

back_blocks.md: A **respirometer** is apparatus used to measure the rate of **oxygen uptake** (gas volume change) by respiring organisms.

front_blocks.md: In a respirometer, what is the role of **potassium hydroxide (KOH)**?

back_blocks.md: It **absorbs carbon dioxide**, so any change in gas volume is due only to **oxygen uptake**.

cards.front_md: In a respirometer, what is the role of **potassium hydroxide (KOH)**?
cards.back_md: It **absorbs carbon dioxide**, so any change in gas volume is due only to **oxygen uptake**.

front_blocks.md: Outline how a respirometer measures the **oxygen uptake** of germinating seeds.

back_blocks.md: Seeds are sealed in a tube with **KOH** to absorb CO<sub>2</sub>.
As O<sub>2</sub> is used up, gas volume falls and the coloured fluid in the manometer moves **towards the seeds**.
The distance moved measures the volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed.

cards.front_md: Outline how a respirometer measures the **oxygen uptake** of germinating seeds.
cards.back_md:
Seeds are sealed in a tube with **KOH** to absorb CO<sub>2</sub>.

As O<sub>2</sub> is used up, gas volume falls and the coloured fluid in the manometer moves **towards the seeds**.

The distance moved measures the volume of O<sub>2</sub> consumed.

front_blocks.md: How is a respirometer used to determine the **RQ** of an organism?

back_blocks.md: Measure O<sub>2</sub> uptake with CO<sub>2</sub> absorbed (KOH present).
Then repeat **without** the CO<sub>2</sub> absorbent to measure the net volume change (CO<sub>2</sub> produced − O<sub>2</sub> used).
Use both readings to calculate RQ = CO<sub>2</sub> produced ÷ O<sub>2</sub> used.

cards.front_md: How is a respirometer used to determine the **RQ** of an organism?
cards.back_md:
Measure O<sub>2</sub> uptake with CO<sub>2</sub> absorbed (KOH present).

Then repeat **without** the CO<sub>2</sub> absorbent to measure the net volume change (CO<sub>2</sub> produced − O<sub>2</sub> used).

Use both readings to calculate RQ = CO<sub>2</sub> produced ÷ O<sub>2</sub> used.

front_blocks.md: Why should a respirometer be kept in a **water bath** at constant temperature?

back_blocks.md: Gas volume changes with temperature.
A constant temperature ensures volume changes are due to **respiration only**.
